source.title: A Universal Trade-off Between the Model Size, Test Loss, and Training Loss of Linear Predictors

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical results on test loss versus model size and training loss for linear predictors, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's results on linear predictors and its Marchenko–Pastur analysis bear on the claim. Results attributed to cited work, including the discussion of regularization attenuating the peak, are not recorded as this paper's results.
record.test_reason: Theory for linear predictors. The paper derives the minimum achievable excess test loss, under a training-loss constraint, as the feature-to-sample ratio varies. It gives an exact asymptotic curve on the overparameterized side (Fig. 1, Thm 3), the peak height at p=n (Thm 5), and shows the loss scales with noise variance σ². These bear on V3, V4 and part of V6 for linear models. The quantity is a minimum over all algorithms, including oracles, not the risk of a specific trained model.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Add three points. The peak at p=n has a 1/τ pole and is discontinuous between interpolating and non-interpolating regimes. The authors call the peak a less robust phenomenon, highly sensitive to regularization. The tail (p≫n) is stable in τ and the general bound is tight there.
record.recipe_differences: The study provides theoretical lower bounds and an asymptotic analysis of constrained linear predictors; it does not reproduce the original deep-network size or training-epoch experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak behavior depends on the training-loss constraint τ and is analyzed under Marchenko–Pastur and linear-model assumptions. The paper notes that the peak is sensitive to regularization, citing prior work.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1: for any algorithm and non-degenerate linear feature map, expected excess loss ≥ σ²(n/p)(1−√τ)². It is tight as p/n→∞ under MP assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear predictors with training loss below the noise level need substantial excess overparameterization to reach near-optimal test loss, whatever the algorithm or distribution.

record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The results are theoretical and restricted to linear predictors; the more precise curve requires Marchenko–Pastur and additive-noise assumptions. The study does not directly test deep networks or training epochs, and it reports no empirical uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Model classes other than linear predictors; the underparameterized classical U-shaped side; the risk of actual algorithms rather than the constrained minimum.
Multiple or triple descent; disappearance of the peak under optimally tuned regularization of a real estimator.

missing.what: Theorem 3: E*(τ,γ)/γ is strictly increasing in γ for τ in (0,1]. This gives the monotone rise of minimum excess loss as n/p → 1, the key result for V3.
Theorem 4 / Eq. (3)/(31): near-interpolation lower bound σ²γ/(1−γ)·(1−√(τ/(1−γ)))², tight up to o(√τ).
Remark 5: the lower bound arises purely from variance due to label noise, via an oracle ridge estimator whose ridge parameter is the training-loss multiplier.

record.verdict_notes: Belkin coauthors this paper but it is not an original source, so verdicts are allowed. All results bound or compute the minimum excess loss over every algorithm meeting a training-loss constraint, including oracles such as β*, not the risk of a trained estimator. Readers should weigh the V3/V4/V6 verdicts accordingly. Fig. 1 shows only the overparameterized side. The 'regularization attenuates the peak' statement for the τ=0 case is cited from [14]; only the finite-τ peak formula is this paper's own result.

versions.untested_parts: The paper analyzes linear predictors, not deep networks.
It does not vary training epochs or training time.
The sample-size behavior is analyzed asymptotically under Marchenko–Pastur and linear-model assumptions, not in deep networks or finite-sample experiments.
The paper's own results concern linear predictors; other model classes are not tested.
The paper does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
It does not test whether noise causes the peak, multiple or triple descent, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization. It discusses regularization effects reported in cited work.
The paper does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that produces an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: p-dimensional linear feature model
rows.operation_detail: Derives a distribution- and algorithm-independent lower bound on excess test loss under a training-loss constraint.

conditions.value: at most τσ² almost surely; τ < 1
n samples, p features; non-degenerate feature map

rows.note: This establishes a lower bound and trade-off, not by itself a fall-rise-fall test-loss curve. It supports the proposed claim: for linear models with training loss below the noise level, good excess test loss requires substantial overparameterization or training loss near the noise level.
rows.check: A non-asymptotic lower bound cannot show a fall-rise-fall curve or that risk actually falls past interpolation. Keep under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: linear predictors under Marchenko–Pastur asymptotics
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes the minimum expected excess loss while varying the sample-to-feature ratio.

conditions.value: Marchenko–Pastur spectral limit; linear optimal model with additive noise

rows.value: E*(τ,γ) = σ²γ[m(−λ;γ) − λm′(−λ;γ)], where λ satisfies λ²m′(−λ;γ) = τ; the plotted exact curves vary with p/n and show a peak near p/n = 1.
rows.note: The asymptotic curve is presented for the minimum achievable excess loss subject to a training-loss constraint, not for an ordinary deep-network training sweep. V3 is supported by the curve as the sample-to-feature ratio approaches the interpolation threshold from the overparameterized side.
rows.check: Fig. 1a covers only γ=n/p in (0,1), the overparameterized side. It shows E* rising toward p=n and falling as p/n grows, but not the underparameterized side. For small τ that side is infeasible (E*=∞ when 1−p/n>τ). The row's 'peak near p/n=1' overstates a full peak. The monotone rise in γ comes from Theorem 3, which should be added to the locator. For V3 alone the state is observed: with p fixed, raising n toward p raises E*. For V6 the loss is proportional to σ².

rows.measure: Minimum expected excess test loss at the interpolation threshold
rows.note: This gives the peak behavior for the specified asymptotic linear setting; it does not establish a peak for deep networks.
rows.check: Gives only the peak height at γ=1, not the curve. The peak is finite for every τ>0 and grows as Θ(1/τ) as τ→0. The authors say it is discontinuous relative to the infinite interpolating peak. This bears on V6 (training-loss level acts as regularization) and on how fragile the peak is.

source_check.correct: For V4, state=cannot_determine: the value at γ=1 alone cannot show post-threshold improvement. For V6, partial is appropriate for the noise and peak-attenuation components.

source_check.problem: A threshold-height result alone does not establish even an incomplete capacity-dependent curve for V4.
